text:
AI routing is like an art of its own ↓

Which model, tool, or policy should handle your request is a job of a router.

AI router can be a set of rules, a classifier, a small neural network, or another language model.

Its decision can work in a few ways:

- Route by task type: e.g., send coding requests to a coding model. But simple, a one-line edit and a difficult bug don’t need the same resources.

- Predict how each candidate will perform on the specific input, using data from previous runs.

- Weigh that predicted quality against cost. The more cost matters, the bigger the quality advantage an expensive model needs to justify its selection.

▪️ But there are some pitfalls on the routing road.

- Choosing the most likely winner isn’t the same as choosing the best expected result. One model may win often but also crash hard. Another may rarely come first but stays consistently strong, or is strong for the specific start.

-  The savings aren’t always worth it: a model may cost one-tenth as much as a perfect model but succeeds only 15% of the time. It produces 50% more correct answers per dollar, but it also fails 85% of the time.

That's why a router may need a quality floor: a minimum level of performance it has to maintain while trying to reduce cost.

@YangYou1991, great work on Route Anything!
@RoyRinberg, great work on FlashProve!

We’ve covered the rest of the details and challenges of routing here, plus how FlashProve and VeriRouter can help verify router's choice and results:
